title: Why Do Bees Matter?
paragraphs: Popular imagination may cast the bee chiefly as a producer of honey, but its true significance, ecological and economic alike, resides in pollination. In the course of foraging, bees convey pollen from anther to stigma, effecting the fertilisation upon which the reproduction of a vast array of flowering plants depends.

Nor is the domesticated honeybee more than a minor protagonist. Some 20,000 bee species have been described, and wild pollinators, bumblebees and solitary bees among them, frequently outperform the honeybee on particular crops, while hoverflies, butterflies, birds and bats complete a remarkably heterogeneous workforce.

International assessments estimate that roughly three quarters of the leading global food crops derive at least some benefit from animal pollination. The great staples, wheat, rice and maize, are wind-pollinated, yet the fruits, vegetables, nuts and seeds that furnish much of our dietary micronutrients and variety are heavily dependent on pollinators, as are lucrative commodities such as coffee and cocoa.

A growing body of evidence documents the decline of numerous pollinator populations, a trend attributable not to any single factor but to a confluence of pressures: the loss and fragmentation of habitat, the expansion of intensive monocultures, exposure to certain pesticides, pathogens and parasites, and a warming climate liable to decouple flowering phenology from insect activity. Any credible response must accordingly operate on several fronts at once, from the restoration of flower-rich landscapes to the reform of agricultural practice.
